Lend

LEND (rhymes with send) · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To let someone use something of yours for a while, knowing you will get it back.

Can you lend me your pencil until lunch?

Worked Example

Maya agreed to lend her bike to Jake for the weekend, and he returned it Monday morning.

Maya let Jake use the bike, but it was still hers, and it came back. Letting someone use your things for a while is lending.

How Lend Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

loan

loan: to lend money or things for a while

share

share: to let others use part of what you have

Antonyms

borrow

borrow: to take a thing you must give back

keep

keep: to hold on to a thing as yours

How Strong Is It? — share → lend → give

share vs. lend

share vs. lend: Share is the milder word: sharing lets others use something along with you for a moment, while lending hands the whole thing over for a while and expects it back.

give vs. lend

give vs. lend: Give goes further than lend: when you lend something, the other person must return it, but when you give something, it belongs to them forever.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — lend

root — lend: to let someone use a thing for a while

Put it together

Put it together: The whole word lend is the root - there is no prefix or suffix to break off. Lend comes from an Old English word and is a cousin of loan. Both words have always been about handing something over for a while and getting it back.

Use the root in a new word: lender

Use the root in a new word: lender: The library is the biggest lender in town: it lets you take books home and expects every one of them back.

Root Check

Word Choice

Lend and borrow are a pair: the owner lends; the taker borrows. 'Can you lend me a pencil?' means the pencil is theirs and will go back to them.
